title: Linguistic Ruin? LOL! Instant Messaging and Teen Language
authors: Sali A. Tagliamonte and Derek Denis
used: Original research abstract: 72 teenagers, over one million IM words, comparison with speech. Reports a mixed register rather than simple linguistic deterioration.
implication: Don't make all 2000s text abbreviated or informal. Select style by medium and relationship.
limit: Abstract inspected; not a global study and not a basis for precise decade-wide frequencies.

title: Features of Digital African American Language in a Social Network Site
used: Original research abstract describes analysis of 1,494 instances in MySpace comments and a combination of digital and African American language features.
implication: Community and platform are explanatory variables. Do not relabel every widely circulated feature as generic youth or Gen Z speech.
limit: Abstract inspected; MySpace community study, not all social media or all Black speakers.

title: It's Complicated: The Social Lives of Networked Teens
used: Publisher summary of original US teen fieldwork on identity, privacy and networked social life; author's open edition located.
implication: Distinguish context and audience from a universal generational personality.
limit: Publisher overview used for context; full book not read in this research. No chapter-level empirical claims are made.

title: Watch the birth of on fleek, live!
used: Contemporary reporting includes direct contact with Peaches Monroee and distinguishes earlier fleek entries from the viral phrase.
implication: Separate a word's existence, a particular phrase's popularization and its broader uptake.
limit: Journalistic provenance evidence, not proof of the first-ever use of every component.

title: Jools Lebron explains her demure example
authors: Analisa Novak and Karina Perez / CBS Mornings
used: Contemporary creator interview explains consideration, presentation and community alongside the viral joke.
implication: Do not flatten a mixed sincere/comic communication into pure irony.
limit: One creator's explanation; does not measure how every participant interpreted the meme.
